<meta>This page contains the start of the Valāhakavagga (Chapter on Thunderclouds) from the Book of Fours in the Aṅguttara Nikāya. It presents a teaching using a metaphor of four types of clouds to categorize four types of people based on their mastery of the scriptures versus their internal realization of the Four Noble Truths.</meta>

->### THE CHAPTER ON THUNDERCLOUDS 103<-

102.

1. Monks, there are these four thunderclouds. Which four?
The one that thunders but does not rain . . . <note>original: pe, a standard abbreviation indicating an ellipsis of repeated text</note> . . . and the one that thunders and rains.
These, monks, are the four thunderclouds.

2. Just so, monks, there are these four <term>puggalā</term> <gloss>persons</gloss> comparable to thunderclouds who are found existing in the world. Which four?
The one who thunders but does not rain . . . <note>indicating the ellipsis of the intermediate categories</note> . . . and the one who thunders and rains.

3. And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>the teaching</gloss>: the <term>Sutta</term> <gloss>discourses</gloss>, <term>Geyya</term> <gloss>mixed prose and verse</gloss>, <term>Veyyākaraṇa</term> <gloss>explanations</gloss>, <term>Gāthā</term> <gloss>verses</gloss>, <term>Udāna</term> <gloss>inspired utterances</gloss>, <term>Itivuttaka</term> <gloss>the "as-it-was-said" quotations</gloss>, <term>Jātaka</term> <gloss>birth stories</gloss>, <term>Abbhutadhamma</term> <gloss>extraordinary accounts</gloss>, and <term>Vedalla</term> <gloss>catechetical analyses</gloss>. Yet he does not understand, as it really is, that "this is <term>dukkha</term> <gloss>suffering</gloss>" . . . <note>indicating the ellipsis of the other Noble Truths: the origin and cessation</note> . . . he does not understand, as it really is, that "this is the <term>dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā</term> <gloss>path leading to the cessation of suffering</gloss>."
In this way, monks, a person thunders but does not rain; monks, I say that this person is comparable to that thundercloud which thunders but does not rain.

4. And how, monks, is a person one who rains but does not thunder?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the <term>Dhamma</term>: the <term>Sutta</term> . . . <note>pe</note> . . . <term>Vedalla</term>. Yet he understands, as it really is, that "this is suffering" . . . <note>pe</note> . . . he understands, as it really is, that "this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, a person rains but does not thunder; monks, I say that [he is comparable to that thundercloud] . . . <note>indicating a repetitive formula</note>.

5. And how, monks, is a person one who neither thunders nor rains?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the <term>Dhamma</term>: the <term>Sutta</term> . . . <term>Vedalla</term>. He does not understand, as it really is, that "this is suffering" . . . the path leading to the cessation of suffering. In this way, monks, [is the person] who neither thunders nor rains; monks, I say that [he is comparable to that thundercloud] . . .

6. And how, monks, is a person one who both thunders and rains?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the <term>Dhamma</term>: the <term>Sutta</term> . . . <term>Vedalla</term>. He understands, as it really is, that "this is suffering" . . . the path leading to the cessation of suffering. In this way, monks, a person both thunders and rains; just like that thundercloud, monks, which both thunders and rains, so do I describe this person.

<summary>This page describes a discourse by the Buddha comparing four types of individuals to four types of thunderclouds, distinguishing between those who study the scriptures and those who realize the Four Noble Truths.</summary>
<keywords>thundercloud metaphor, four types of persons, ninefold Dhamma, Four Noble Truths, mastery of scripture, internal realization</keywords>
